questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT typically associated with school refusal?
questions.explanation: School refusal is characterised by refusal to go to school or stay in school, even when under pressure from parents and school authorities. It is not a psychiatric disorder per se and can have many causes; it is considered a problem rather than a diagnosis. School refusal is generally associated with separation anxiety and may co-occur with anxiety and depressive disorders. It is usually not an isolated problem. These children typically avoid many other social situations, and often display tantrums, desperate pleas, and somatic complaints (e.g. headaches, stomach aches, nausea). School refusal may occur in a young child who is Xrst entering school or in an older child or adolescent who is making a transition into a new grade or school. Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition.2022. p. 896.Elliott JG, Place M. Practitioner review: school refusal: developments inconceptualisation and treatment since 2000. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry. 2019 Jan;60(1):4-15.

questions.question_text: Which of the following childhood psychiatric conditions has the highest heritability factor?
questions.explanation: ADHD has the highest heritability among the listed conditions. ADHD has a heritability of 70-80%, and the risk of ADHD in siblings is 2-3x increased. Rates are increased in premature babies (especially extreme prematurity), babies born to mothers who used substances during pregnancy (e.g. tobacco or alcohol), following head injury, and in some genetic and metabolic disorders. None of the proposed prenatal risk factors have been conXrmed as causal for ADHD.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 668.Sciberras E, Mulraney M, Silva D, Coghill D. Prenatal risk factors and the etiology of ADHD—review of existing evidence. Current psychiatry reports. 2017 Jan 1;19(1):1.

questions.question_text: When compared to younger children, which one of the following features of depression is seen more commonly in older children and adolescents?
questions.explanation: Younger children (ages 3-8) with depression may have trouble verbalising feelings but show marked decreased interest in play, increased somatic complaints, and crying or shouting outbursts. Older children and adolescents (ages 9-18) with depression may have low self-esteem, guilt, hopelessness, increased boredom, feelings of wanting to run away, and decreased grades and poor school performance.Ref: Mullen S. Major depressive disorder in children and adolescents. Mental Health Clinician. 2018 Nov;8(6):275-83.

questions.question_text: In children with PANDAS, which of the following is least common?
questions.explanation: Paediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorder associated with streptococcal infections (PANDAS) is characterised by the sudden and dramatic onset of obsessive-compulsive disorder, tic symptoms, or severely restricted food intake and neuropsychiatric comorbidity, also of sudden and severe onset, following group A streptococci (GAS) infection. Common comorbidities include anxiety (including separation anxiety); emotional lability and/or depression; irritability, aggression and/or severely oppositional behaviours; behavioural (developmental) regression; deterioration in school performance (ADHD-like symptoms, memory deXcits, cognitive changes); sensory or motor abnormalities; somatic signs and symptoms (including sleep disturbances, enuresis, or increased urinary frequency). Nearly ⅓ of children endorse concerns related to suicide. The term Pediatric Acute-onset Neuropsychiatric Syndrome (PANS) is used when the etiology or mechanism of the abrupt onset is unknown.Ref: Warrilow A, Morton M. Autoimmune disorders in child psychiatry: keeping up with the Xeld. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Nov;21(6):367-76.Cabrera-Mendoza B et al. Diagnosis in PANDAS: An Update. Current Psychiatry Research and Reviews Formerly: Current Psychiatry Reviews. 2019 Dec 1;15(4):237-47.

questions.question_text: About 99% of children are dry by day (no daytime wetting) by the age of
questions.explanation: By the age of 5 years, only 1% of children have problems with daytime wetting. However, nocturnal enuresis can still alect 15-22% boys and 7-15% girls at the age of 7 years. questions.question_text: Which of the following is considered the treatment of choice for children with school refusal?
questions.explanation: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) continues to be the therapy of choice for school refusal (with a shift in emphasis over time from standardised to individualised approaches, and the incorporation of exposure techniques). CBT has largely replaced psychoanalytic approaches as the preferred method of treatment for school refusal. While it seems that family work is an essential aspect of treatment for school refusal, controlled studies examining family-based therapies have been rare and Xndings have been equivocal. Instead, family work is now seen as more appropriately embedded within a CBT programme. There is little evidenceto support the use of medication as part of a treatment programme for school refusal.Of note, a continuing divide exists between those who argue for and against aconceptual merger in which the term 'school refusal' or 'school refusal behaviour'includes both those anxious about attending school, and those who wouldhistorically be classed as 'truants'. Some commentators have queried whetherthose labelled as truants are treated less sympathetically than those whosenonattendance is considered to be the consequence of high levels of anxiety. Theimpact of labelling can result in dilerential access to professional services, and forms of intervention, with truancy often more likely to result in legal proceedingsthat may reoect a punitive, rather than a therapeutic, focus.Ref: Elliott JG, Place M. Practitioner review: school refusal: developments inconceptualisation and treatment since 2000. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry. 2019 Jan;60(1):4-15.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true about Tourette syndrome?

options.text: Mean age of onset is 12 years
Females are more alected than males
Diagnosed by having both motor and vocal tics for 6 months
Diagnosed by having both motor and vocal tics for 12 months
Antipsychotics are the Xrst line treatment

correct_answer.text: Diagnosed by having both motor and vocal tics for 12 months

correct_answers.text: Diagnosed by having both motor and vocal tics for 12 months

questions.explanation: Tourette syndrome is a complex neuropsychiatric disorder with childhood onset characterised by multiple motor and one or more vocal tics, present for at least ayear. Males are more commonly alected (3-4:1, male:female). The age of onset is 2-21 years, with a mean age of 7 years. All patients should receive psychoeducation,reassurance, and explanation. In mild cases and young people this may supce.Behavioural methods (that may be useful alone or in combination with medications) include habit reversal training, comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, exposure and response prevention, and self-hypnosis.Medication is warranted if tics cause distress or are functionally disabling and isalso used in the treatment of many of the co-morbidities.Ref: Robertson MM. Tourette syndrome in children and adolescents: aetiology,presentation and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2016 May;22(3):165-75.Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines inPsychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 587.

questions.question_text: Blockade of which of the following receptors can reduce vocal and motor tics seen in Tourette syndrome?
questions.explanation: Evidence suggests that dopamine super-sensitivity, speciXcally involving nigrostriatal dopamine D2 receptors, leads to tics. Agents that reduce dopamineactivity suppress tics, while dopamine-enhancing substances (like cocaine)exacerbate them.Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 444.Nomura Y. Pharmacological therapy for Tourette syndrome: What medicine can do and cannot do. Biomedical Journal. 2021 Sep 20.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is thought to have the least genetic loading/heritability?
questions.explanation: Of those listed, conduct disorder is thought to have the least genetic loading. Still, there is now solid evidence from twin and adoption studies that conduct problems assessed both dimensionally and categorically are substantially heritable.Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on therecognition, intervention and management of antisocial behaviour and conductdisorders in children and young people. Updated 2017.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a true statement about bipolar disorder in children and adolescents?

options.text: 60-70% of initial presentations are a manic episode
Manic children typically present with atypical or mixed features
Lamotrigine is used if treatment resistant manic episodes are present
The course is often episodic and of brief duration

correct_answer.text: Manic children typically present with atypical or mixed features

correct_answers.text: Manic children typically present with atypical or mixed features

questions.explanation: Children experiencing a manic episode typically present with atypical or mixed features characterised by irritability, labile mood, and behavioural problems.Periods of depression are common, and early-onset bipolar disorder more oftenpresents with depression than in adult-onset bipolar. Early-onset bipolar may becharacterised by non-episodic, chronic, ultra-rapid cycling, mixed irritable andmanic states. The prevalence in adolescents is approximately 1% and as high as 6%when including soft subsyndromal symptoms. M>F in childhood cases; M=F inadolescents. For the treatment of mania and hypomania in youth, NICE guidelinessuggest following the same recommendations as adults: second-generationantipsychotics (SGAs) may be used as Xrst-line treatment, and mood stabilisers canbe added after failure of two trials of SGAs. Lamotrigine has not been studied inRCTs for the treatment of acute bipolar depression in children and adolescents andis not recommended as Xrst-line. It is not recommended in the treatment of manicepisodes.Ref: Findling RL et al. Progress in diagnosis and treatment of bipolar disorder among children and adolescents: an international perspective. Evidence-based mental health. 2018 Nov 1;21(4):177-81.National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on theassessment and management of bipolar disorder in adults, children and youngpeople in primary and secondary care. Updated edition 2020.Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines inPsychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 547-551.

questions.question_text: Which of the following treatments is most recommended for treating PTSD in children?
questions.explanation: Within one month of a traumatic event, consider active monitoring or individual trauma-focused CBT for children and adolescents. >1 month after a traumatic event, the treatment of choice for PTSD is individual trauma-focused CBT. Consider EMDR for those ages 7-17 who present >3 months after a traumatic event only if they do not respond to or engage with trauma-focused CBT. Do NOT use psychologically-focused debrieXng for the prevention or treatment of PTSD in children and adolescents. Do NOT oler drug treatments for the prevention ortreatment of PTSD in children and young people under 18 years.Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. NICE guideline Post-traumatic stress disorder 2018.

questions.explanation: 80% of patients with autism have mild to moderate intellectual disability. questions.question_text: Which of the following blood abnormalities is commonly seen in anorexia nervosa?
questions.explanation: Anaemia, leukopenia, and although less frequently, thrombocytopaenia arepossible haematological complications of anorexia nervosa (AN) considered strictlysecondary to chronic malnutrition. Usually, anaemia in AN is normocytic andnormochromic, and leukopenia is characterised by lymphocytopenia orneutropenia; thrombocytopaenia may also be present.Ref: De Filippo E et al. Hematological complications in anorexia nervosa. EuropeanJournal of Clinical Nutrition. 2016 Nov;70(11):1305-8.

questions.question_text: What is the average age of onset of schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: The average age of onset of schizophrenia is 23 years of age in men and 26 years ofage in women.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 190.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about suicide and adolescents is true?

options.text: 1% of adolescents who attempt suicide repeat within a year.
Hanging is the most common method of suicide in UK adolescents.
Suicide is the leading cause of death amongst adolescents.
Female suicides are more than male suicides in UK adolescents.
Most Xrst attempts at suicide by adolescents are pre-planned.

correct_answer.text: Hanging is the most common method of suicide in UK adolescents.

correct_answers.text: Hanging is the most common method of suicide in UK adolescents.

questions.explanation: Rates of suicide in the UK have increased among adolescents by approximately7.9% each year between 2010 and 2017. Rates among females have increased at ahigher rate, though absolute number of deaths is still lower among young womenthan young men. Suicide is the third leading cause of death for adolescents,following accidents and homicides. Hanging is the most common method of suicidein the UK for both children and adolescents. Half of suicide attempts are Xrstattempts and most are impulsive, with only 25% having evidence of planning(impulsivity is linked to sensation-seeking and increased risk-taking behaviour inadolescence). 10% of adolescents who attempt suicide repeat within a year. Ref: Correia R, Jackson D. Risk to self: identifying and managing risk of suicide andself-harm. BJPsych Advances. 2020:1-11.Bould H et al. Rising suicide rates among adolescents in England and Wales. TheLancet. 2019 Jul 13;394(10193):116-7.Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019Jul 30. pp. 698-699.

questions.question_text: The most common psychiatric emergency seen in the child and adolescent population is
questions.explanation: Numerous reasons are given for emergency presentations, but most commonly thegoal is the assessment of self-injurious thoughts and behaviours (SITB). In additionto non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI), which is carried out without the intention to die,suicidal behaviour, in which the person has at least to some degree the intention todie, is deXned as SITB. Since the intention to die is often ambivalent in patients,there is overlap between NSSI and suicidal behaviour.Ref: Kandsperger S et al. Suicidality presented to a child and adolescent psychiatryemergency service: increasing rate and changing characteristics. Frontiers inpsychiatry. 2021:1195.

questions.question_text: Preschoolers and school-age children who stutter exhibit an increased incidence of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Very young children who stutter typically show some delay in the development oflanguage and articulation without additional disorders of speech and language.Preschoolers and school-age children who stutter exhibit an increased incidence ofsocial anxiety, school refusal, and other anxiety symptoms. Older children whostutter also do not necessarily have co-morbid speech and language disorders, butoften manifest anxiety symptoms and disorders. When stuttering persists intoadolescence, social isolation occurs at higher rates than in the general adolescentpopulation.Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition.2022. p. 118.

questions.question_text: The overall prevalence of psychiatric problems in adolescence is
questions.explanation: Adolescence, deXned as a transitional phase between ages 10 and 19, is sometimesperceived as a phase of life with no health problems. However, approximately 20%of adolescents experience a mental health problem, most commonly depression oranxiety.Ref: Silva SA et al. Common mental disorders prevalence in adolescents: Asystematic review and meta-analyses. PloS one. 2020 Apr 23;15(4):e0232007.

questions.question_text: With appropriate consultation and monitoring, which of the following medications can be prescribed for children with ADHD and congenital heart disease?
questions.explanation: Children with congenital heart disease (CHD) have been shown to be at increasedrisk for ADHD. Case reports have led to concern regarding the use of ADHDmedications in children with underlying CHD. However, multiple large studies havedemonstrated no increased risk of sudden cardiac death in children on stimulantmedications or atomoxetine. Typical cardiovascular changes are a mild increase inheart rate and/or blood pressure that are rarely haemodynamically signiXcant.Prior to prescribing, an ECG and cardiology opinion should be sought if the patienthas a history of CHD.Ref: Pierick AR et al. Treatment of attention deXcit/hyperactivity disorder in childrenwith CHD. Cardiology in the Young. 2021 Jun;31(6):969-72.Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines inPsychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 570.

questions.question_text: Which autoimmune disorder is associated with OCD in children?
questions.explanation: Paediatric autoimmune neuropsychiatric disorder associated with streptococcalinfections (PANDAS) is characterised by the sudden and dramatic onset ofobsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), tic symptoms, or severely restricted foodintake and neuropsychiatric comorbidity, also of sudden and severe onset,following group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal (GABHS) infection. Thepathophysiological hypothesis in PANDAS states that GABHS infections trigger theproduction of antibodies that, in turn, cross-react against the central nervoussystem and cause tics and OCD symptoms. In contrast to Tourette syndrome,where a preceding infection may exacerbate symptoms, in PANDAS thestreptococcal infection and its induced cross-reacting antibodies are proposed asthe cause of the symptoms. The term Pediatric Acute-onset NeuropsychiatricSyndrome (PANS) is used when the aetiology or mechanism of the abrupt onset isunknown.Ref: Warrilow A, Morton M. Autoimmune disorders in child psychiatry: keeping upwith the Xeld. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Nov;21(6):367-76.Cabrera-Mendoza B et al. Diagnosis in PANDAS: An Update. questions.question_text: In the aetiology of disruptive behaviour disorders (DBDs; including oppositional deXant disorder and conduct disorder), which of the following statements regarding parenting styles is true?

options.text: Parenting styles are not key factors in shaping DBDs in children
Harsh parenting is not associated with DBDs in children and adolescents
When siblings live together in the same family, they experience the same parenting
If one child in a family has DBD, their sibling(s) will also have DBD
The presence of DBD in a family is a risk factor for externalising problems insiblings

correct_answer.text: The presence of DBD in a family is a risk factor for externalising problems insiblings

correct_answers.text: The presence of DBD in a family is a risk factor for externalising problems insiblings

questions.explanation: Studies have indicated that parenting styles are key factors in shaping disruptivebehaviour disorders (DBDs; including oppositional deXant disorder and conductdisorder) in children. SpeciXcally, the use of harsh parenting, which includescoercive, controlling, and punitive methods, the use of verbal and physicalaggression, combined with low warmth and poor positive parenting, are associatedwith DBDs as well as more general externalising disorders in children andadolescents. Even when siblings live in the same family context, they canexperience dilerent relationships with the same parents, and be exposed todilerent levels of harsh and supporting parenting, thus resulting in dilerentadjustments. The clinical manifestation of DBDs (which includes irritability,aggression, and temper outbursts) is a risk factor for the development ofexternalising problems in siblings.Ref: Smorti M et al. Parenting and sibling relationships in family with disruptivebehavior disorders. Are non-clinical siblings more vulnerable for emotional andbehavioral problems?. Brain Sciences. 2021 Oct 1;11(10):1308.

questions.question_text: In operant conditioning with children, shaping refers to

options.text: Reinforcing positive behaviour; ignoring negative behaviour
Punishing negative behaviour; praising positive behaviour
Neither reinforcing nor punishing observed behaviours
Gradual reinforcement of behaviours approximating the desired outcome
Dilerential reinforcement of behaviours other than the desired outcome

correct_answer.text: Gradual reinforcement of behaviours approximating the desired outcome

correct_answers.text: Gradual reinforcement of behaviours approximating the desired outcome

questions.explanation: Shaping is used to produce a complex behaviour that is not in the child's initialrepertoire. Initially, component parts of the desired behaviour are rewarded, thenreward is limited to behaviour that approximates the desired outcome. Asappropriate behaviour appears, it is rewarded only if it is 'in the right direction', andfurther reward is contingent upon continued advancement until the child is onlyrewarded once the entire behaviour is performed.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 907.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs has the best evidence for use in childhood depression?
questions.explanation: UK guidelines (particularly NICE, updated 2019) recommend a stepped-careapproach in the treatment of childhood depression. 5–11-year-old children shouldonly be olered ouoxetine when psychological therapy has been inelective.Second-line medications are sertraline and citalopram. Paroxetine and venlafaxineshould not be used, as they have the strongest association with suicide risk(especially with adolescents). TCAs should not be used; they are not useful in youngchildren and there is only low-quality marginal evidence to support their use inadolescents.Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on theidentiXcation and management of depression in children and young people. 2019.

questions.question_text: Most children with selective mutism also meet diagnostic criteria for which of the following disorders?
questions.explanation: Selective mutism is characterised by the persistent failure to speak in speciXcsettings (e.g. school) where there is an expectation to speak. It begins after normalspeech has been acquired, and there is full use of language at home/with family.Patients may remain wholly silent or near-silent, in some cases only whispering in aschool setting. In rare cases, a child is mute at home but not in school. Socialanxiety is almost always present.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 687.Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition.2022. p. 201.

questions.question_text: Reactive attachment disorder is generally diagnosed before the age of
questions.explanation: Reactive attachment disorder (RAD) is characterised by grossly abnormalattachment behaviours in early childhood, occurring in the context of a history ofgrossly inadequate child care (e.g. severe neglect, maltreatment, institutionaldeprivation). Even when an adequate primary caregiver is newly available, the childdoes not turn to the primary caregiver for comfort, support, and nurture; rarelydisplays security-seeking behaviours towards any adult; and does not respondwhen comfort is olered. RAD can only be diagnosed in children, and features ofthe disorder develop within the Xrst 5 years of life. However, the disorder cannotbe diagnosed before the age of 1 (or a developmental age of less than 9 months),when the capacity for selective attachments may not be fully developed, or in thecontext of autism spectrum disorder.Ref: International Statistical ClassiXcation of Diseases and Related Health Problems(11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is considered a protective factor against the development ofconduct problems in high-risk children?

options.text: Learning problems before 10 years of age
Having a family member convicted for violent conduct

questions.explanation: Werner's Kauai Longitudinal Study monitored the impact of a variety of biologicaland psychosocial risk factors, stressful life events, and protective factors on thedevelopment of a multiethnic cohort of 698 children born in 1955 on the 'GardenIsland' in the Hawaiian chain. Some 30% of the survivors in the study populationwere considered high-risk children because they were born in chronic poverty,subjected to perinatal stress, and lived in family environments troubled by chronicdiscord, divorce, or parental psychopathology. The Xndings focused on resiliencyresiliencyresiliencyresiliencyand its contribution to good developmental outcomes despite high-risk status.Ref: Werner EE. Resilience in development. Current directions in psychologicalscience. 1995 Jun;4(3):81-4.

questions.question_text: Regarding the aetiology of ADHD, all of the following are true except

options.text: There is a 50% increased risk in monozygotic twins
Siblings of hyperactive children have about twice the increased risk of having the disorder
Predominant serotonin dysregulation is seen in the prefrontal cortex
Neuroimaging shows lower cerebral blood oow and metabolic rates in thefrontal lobe areas of children with ADHD than in controls

correct_answer.text: Predominant serotonin dysregulation is seen in the prefrontal cortex

correct_answers.text: Predominant serotonin dysregulation is seen in the prefrontal cortex

questions.explanation: Many neurotransmitters are likely associated with ADHD symptoms. However,dopamine is a primary focus of clinical investigation, and the prefrontal cortex hasbeen implicated based on its role in attention and regulation of impulse control.Studies have also shown that brain regions such as the locus coeruleus, whichconsists predominantly of noradrenergic neurons, play a signiXcant role inattention. In part, hypotheses regarding the neurochemistry of ADHD have arisenfrom the elect of medications. Stimulants, known to be the most electivemedications in the treatment of ADHD, alect both dopamine and norepinephrine,leading to neurotransmitter hypotheses that may include dysfunction in both theadrenergic and dopaminergic systems.Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition.2022. p. 139.

questions.question_text: Which of the following suggests a diagnosis of bulimia nervosa rather than anorexia nervosa?
questions.explanation: There is an increased prevalence of disorders of impulsivity and lack of control inpeople with bulimia nervosa. Patients who have to satisfy their binges at all costs(e.g. shoplifting) may have issues with impulsivity and rage. People with bulimicillnesses also have a higher prevalence of substance misuse.Ref: Morris J, Anderson S. An update on eating disorders. BJPsych Advances. 2020:1-11.

questions.question_text: Pica typically occurs during
questions.explanation: Pica is characterised by the persistent (>1month) eating of non-nutritive substancesat a developmentally inappropriate age (>1 year). It typically occurs during the 2and 3 years of life, though may occur in young pregnant women. Commonsubstances include dirt, stones, plastic, paper, hair, faeces, wood, string, etc. Pica iscommon in people with intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder.Consequences may include toxicity, infection, or GIT ulceration/obstruction.Hypothesized causes include hunger, malnutrition, nutritional deXciencies,psychosocial stressors, and brain disorders such as lesions in the hypothalamus.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 694.

questions.question_text: A 14-year-old girl presents with some uncoordinated movements of her limbs andemotional lability. She has a history of fever and sore throat six months ago. Whichis the most likely cause for her presentation?
questions.explanation: Sydenham chorea is the major neurological presentation of rheumatic fever, an inflammatory process following infection with group A streptococci (GAS) such as throat infection or scarlet fever. Sydenham chorea is characterised by uncoordinated jerking movements alecting the face and limbs, as well as hypotonia. Some children also experience vocal and motor tics that may persist. Behavioural symptoms and psychiatric co-morbidities are common and can have an abrupt onset that may precede the onset of the chorea. Emotional lability, anxiety, and symptoms of OCD are the most well recognised and there have also been associations with ADHD, mood disorders, and even symptoms of psychosis.Ref: Warrilow A, Morton M. Autoimmune disorders in child psychiatry: keeping up with the Xeld. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Nov;21(6):367-76.

questions.question_text: Which of the following treatments is no longer licensed in the UK for children with ADHD?
questions.explanation: Pemoline is no longer licensed in UK because of the risk of serious hepatotoxicityand death.Ref: Safer DJ, Zito JM, Gardner JF. Pemoline hepatotoxicity and postmarketingsurveillance. Journal of the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry.2001 Jun 1;40(6):622-9.

questions.question_text: Which drug is now speciXcally contraindicated in depressed children and adolescents due to an association with increased risk of suicide?
questions.explanation: Paroxetine and venlafaxine should not be used for the treatment of depression inchildren and young people, as they have the strongest association with suicide risk.Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on theidentiXcation and management of depression in children and young people. 2019.

questions.question_text: The most common cause of co-morbidity in children and adolescents with bipolar disorder is
questions.explanation: Amongst children and adolescents with bipolar disorder, approximately 53% haveADHD, 42% ODD, 23% an anxiety disorder, 27% conduct disorder, and 9% asubstance disorder.Ref: Findling RL et al. Progress in diagnosis and treatment of bipolar disorderamong children and adolescents: an international perspective. Evidence-basedmental health. 2018 Nov 1;21(4):177-81.

questions.question_text: Manifestations of oppositional deXant disorder are almost invariably present

options.text: In the presence of all adults

questions.explanation: In oppositional deXant disorder (ODD), a child's temper outbursts, active refusal tocomply with rules, and annoying behaviours exceed expectations for thesebehaviours for children of the same age. The disorder is an enduring pattern ofnegativistic, hostile, and deXant behaviours in the absence of signiXcant violationsof the rights of others. Manifestations of ODD are almost invariably present in invariably present in invariably present in invariably present inthe homethe homethe homethe home, but they may not be present at school or with other adults or peers. Insome cases, the child has symptoms outside the home from the start. In others, itstarts at home and later moves beyond that. Typically, symptoms of the disorderare most evident in interactions with adults or peers whom the child knows well.Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition.2022. p. 187.

questions.question_text: The most common co-morbid disorders seen in Tourette syndrome are
questions.explanation: 90% of patients with Tourette syndrome have at least one co-morbidity. questions.question_text: The most common co-morbidity in children with Tourette syndrome is
questions.explanation: 90% of patients with Tourette syndrome have at least one co-morbidity. Up to 55%of patients are also diagnosed with ADHD, 50% with OCD, and up to 20% with co-morbid autism spectrum disorder. Males are more likely to have co-morbiddisorders than females. While inchildren, ADHD, ASD, OCD, and oppositional deXant disorder (ODD) are morecommon, in adults the predominant comorbidities are OCD and mood disorders.

questions.question_text: Which of the following has been found to be elective in treating adolescent inhalant abuse?
questions.explanation: Adolescent inhalant abuse is characterised by the use of gases, glues, and/oraerosols to achieve intoxication. Inhalants are frequently one of the Xrst drugs to be used by adolescents due to ease of access, lack of penalties association with possession, and rapid onset of elects. First-line treatment for adolescent inhalant abuse is multimodal, including individual CBT, family therapy, and activity and engagement programs.Ref: Nguyen J, O'Brien C, Schapp S. Adolescent inhalant use prevention,assessment, and treatment: A literature synthesis. International Journal of DrugPolicy. 2016 May 1;31:15-24.

questions.question_text: Which of the following should be used as a Xrst choice treatment in adolescents with acute manic or mixed episodes?
questions.explanation: Aripiprazole and lithium are the only licensed medications for treating mania. Inpractice, lithium is not generally used acutely in the treatment of manic/mixed episodes in adolescents, as it requires commitment to longer-term treatment and regular blood tests. NICE guidelines (updated 2020) recommend considering aripiprazole or using an alternative antipsychotic (e.g. risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine) in accordance with guidance for adults and limiting drug treatment to 12 weeks. It is unclear whether valproate has the same beneXcial elects on maniain young people as it does in adults. NICE recommends that valproatemonotherapy should NOT be used for Xrst-line management of mania and it shouldNOT be olered to girls or young women of childbearing potential because of teratogenic elects and the risk of polycystic ovary syndrome.Ref: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. questions.question_text: Which neurotransmitter system is commonly postulated to be involved in theaetiology of Tourette syndrome?
questions.explanation: The aetiology of Tourette syndrome includes genetic factors and environmentalinouences (infections and neuroimmunological elects, pre- and/or perinataldipculties, psychosocial stressors, and androgen inouences). No single gene hasbeen identiXed (likely more than one gene). An association with psychosocial stressis well known. Heightened HPA axis and noradrenergic system reactivity have beendemonstrated. There is a likely disturbance of the dopamine system. Otheraetiological possibilities include gestational and perinatal insults, exposure toandrogens, heat, fatigue, and post-infectious autoimmune mechanisms.Ref: Robertson MM. Tourette syndrome in children and adolescents: aetiology,presentation and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2016 May;22(3):165-75.Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. questions.question_text: Which of the following is the evidence-based, Xrst-line treatment for OCD inchildren?
questions.explanation: Children with OCD and mild functional impairment should initially be olered self-help guides. If self-help does not work, or for those with mild-moderateimpairment, CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP) should be oleredXrst-line. CBT interventions include learning about the nature of intrusive thoughts,exposure to worrying or disturbing thoughts (obsessions), and Xnding out how thecycles of behaviour and emotions cause the repetitive behaviours (compulsions) topersist. If CBT is inadequate, or for those with severe impairment, medicationshould be added. Combination therapy (CBT plus SSRI) has not been shown to bemore elective than CBT alone, regardless of initial symptom severity. However,combination therapy is more elective than an SSRI alone.Ref: Öst LG, Riise EN, Wergeland GJ, Hansen B, Kvale G. Cognitive behavioral andpharmacological treatments of OCD in children: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Anxiety Disorders. 2016 Oct 1;43:58-69.National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. questions.question_text: The commonest age of presentation for school refusal is
questions.explanation: School refusal is characterised by refusal to go to school or stay in school, evenwhen under pressure from parents and school authorities. It is not a psychiatricdisorder per se and can have many causes; it is considered a problem rather than adiagnosis. School refusal may occur in a young child who is Xrst entering school orin an older child or adolescent who is making a transition into a new grade orschool. The peak age is 11-13 years. questions.question_text: All of the following are risk factors for adolescent suicide except
questions.explanation: Rates of suicide in the UK have increased among adolescents by approximately7.9% each year between 2010 and 2017. Rates among females have increased at ahigher rate, though absolute number of deaths is still lower among young womenthan young men. Completed suicide is more common in males, while suicideattempts and self-harm are more common in females. Other risk factors foradolescent suicide include depression, struggles with sexuality or gender,aggression and impulsivity, dipculties in peer relationships, family dipculties, sleepdipculties, history of self-harm and/or attempted suicide, parentalpsychopathology & suicidal behaviour, and substance misuse (including alcohol).Ref: Correia R, Jackson D. questions.question_text: Developmentally inappropriate social relatedness seen before the age of 5 following prolonged separation from caregivers is seen in
questions.explanation: Disinhibited social engagement disorder is newly described in both DSM-5 and ICD-11. These children maydisplay reduced/absent reticence in approaching/interacting with unfamiliar adults;overly familiar verbal of physical behaviour; diminished/absent checking back withan adult caregiver; and willingness to go ol with unfamiliar adults with little to nohesitation. These children have experienced patterns of extremes of insupcientcare (e.g. social neglect or deprivation, repeated changes of primary caregivers,rearing in institutions or other settings that severely limit opportunities to formselective attachment).Ref: International Statistical ClassiXcation of Diseases and Related Health Problems(11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: Along with emotional disorders, the most common psychiatric disorder(s) seen inchildhood in the Isle of Wight studies was/were
